prompt.context: In the 1960s, PanAm had a monopoly on routes within the United States from the West Coast to the East Coast. These routes originated from three points on the West Coast — Seattle, San Francisco, and Los Angeles — with terminating points in NYC, Washington DC, and Atlanta. (See Exhibit 1.)
prompt.question: The airline was presented with the option to introduce a stopover point in Kansas City. (See Exhibit 2.) 1. Why would the airline want to do this? 2. If the load factor is 50% on all of PanAm's routes from West to East, what will be their new load factor from Kansas City to the East Coast if they now stop in Kansas City? 3. What if the load factor was 80%? 4. At which point does the load factor become irrelevant (i.e., consolidation of aircraft will not be economically beneficial)? 5. Based on the above calculations, what does this suggest about PanAm's decision? 6. What recommendations would you make to management?

clarifying_info.q: Would PanAm pick up additional passengers in Kansas City?
clarifying_info.a: No additional passengers are picked up from Kansas City.

clarifying_info.q: Would PanAm pick up additional cargo in Kansas City?
clarifying_info.a: No additional cargo is picked up.

clarifying_info.q: Is Kansas City intended to become a new hub?
clarifying_info.a: No — Kansas City is a small market, no need for a new hub.

clarifying_info.q: What type of aircraft is used? Can smaller/shorter-range planes be used?
clarifying_info.a: The same plane is used on all routes.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current load factor on West Coast to East Coast routes?
How many seats does each plane have?
clarifying_info.a: Assume 100 seats per plane (the math generalizes to any seat count).

clarifying_info.q: Is demand evenly distributed across the three originating cities?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, assume equal distribution across Seattle, SFO, and LAX.

exhibits.title: Current Routes
exhibits.shows: A route map showing PanAm's current direct routes from three West Coast origins (Seattle, SFO, LAX) each flying directly to three East Coast destinations (NYC, Washington DC, Atlanta) — nine routes in total with no intermediate stops.
exhibits.data: Origins: Seattle, SFO, LAX; Destinations: NYC, Washington DC, Atlanta; 9 direct nonstop routes, no intermediate city

exhibits.title: Proposed Routes
exhibits.shows: A revised route map adding Kansas City as an intermediate stopover point between the West Coast origins and the East Coast destinations.
exhibits.data: Origins: Seattle, SFO, LAX; Intermediate: Kansas City; Destinations: NYC, Washington DC, Atlanta; routes now pass through Kansas City

framework: Understand current route structure and load factor context
Identify the strategic rationale for a Kansas City stopover (load consolidation)
Quantify new load factors under the stopover scenario at 50% and 80%
Determine the break-even load factor threshold above which consolidation is no longer beneficial
Evaluate strategic implications and make a recommendation

questions.prompt: Why would PanAm want to introduce a stopover in Kansas City?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm several hypotheses and then identify load factor consolidation as the critical driver. Acceptable ideas include: using shorter-range planes (ruled out — same plane on all routes), picking up additional passengers (ruled out — no KC passengers), picking up cargo (ruled out), opening a new hub (ruled out — KC is small). The key insight is that at 50% load factor, planes are half-empty. By funneling multiple West Coast routes through KC, PanAm can consolidate passengers onto fewer aircraft for the KC-to-East-Coast leg, improving utilization. Candidate should proactively ask for the load factor figure.

questions.prompt: If load factor is 50% on all West-to-East routes, what is the new load factor from Kansas City to the East Coast after introducing the KC stopover?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use a shortcut: analyze all three routes from ONE West Coast city, then extrapolate. From a single origin (e.g., Seattle) flying to NYC, Washington, and Atlanta — each plane is at 50 seats occupied (50% of 100). After all three West Coast planes stop in KC heading to, say, NYC, there are 3 planes each with 50 passengers = 150 passengers total, but now heading to one destination. These 150 passengers can fit in 2 planes of 100 seats (150/200 = 75% load factor). The new load factor KC to each East Coast city is 75%.

math.setup: 3 West Coast origins each at 50% load (50 passengers per plane, 100-seat aircraft), all stopping in KC and continuing to one East Coast destination.
steps: Total passengers per East Coast destination from all 3 origins = 3 × 50 = 150
Planes needed at 100 seats each = ceil(150/100) = 2 planes
math.answer: New load factor KC to East Coast = 75%

questions.prompt: What if the load factor on all routes was 80%? What is the new KC-to-East-Coast load factor?
questions.guidance: Same approach: 3 origins × 80 passengers = 240 passengers per East Coast destination. At 100 seats per plane, 3 planes are needed (240/300 = 80%). The load factor remains 80% — consolidation does not reduce the number of aircraft needed. Candidate should note this is the same as the original load factor, so no consolidation benefit is achieved.

math.setup: 3 West Coast origins each at 80% load (80 passengers per 100-seat plane).
steps: Total passengers per East Coast destination = 3 × 80 = 240
math.answer: Load factor stays at 80% — no reduction in aircraft needed

questions.prompt: At which load factor does consolidation become irrelevant (i.e., three planes are still needed for the KC-to-East-Coast leg)?
questions.guidance: Consolidation is beneficial as long as 3 West Coast planes (each partly filled) can be merged into 2 planes after KC. This breaks down once total passengers exceed 2 planes' capacity. 3 origins × x% load × 100 seats > 200 seats means x > 66.7%. So above a 66.7% load factor on each West Coast route, three planes are still needed KC to East Coast and consolidation yields no aircraft savings.

math.setup: Find the load factor threshold x at which 3 origins fill more than 2 planes of 100 seats.
steps: Above 66.7% load factor, 3 planes are still required KC to East Coast
math.answer: Break-even threshold = 66.7% load factor. Above this, consolidation is not economically beneficial.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should PanAm consider when deciding whether to proceed with the Kansas City stopover?

categories.name: Load factor trends
ideas: Will load factors on West Coast routes increase beyond 66.7% in the near future, eroding the consolidation benefit?
Historical demand trends on these routes

categories.name: Growth opportunities in Kansas City
ideas: Are there future opportunities to expand KC as a hub or add new routes?
Is KC traffic likely to grow enough to justify the stopover infrastructure?

categories.name: Operational costs
ideas: Additional landing fees and ground handling costs at KC
Increased flight time and fuel costs due to the stop

categories.name: Passenger experience
ideas: Increased travel time may reduce demand on these routes
Risk of passenger leakage to non-stop competitors

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: Do competitors operate direct routes that would become relatively more attractive?
Regulatory considerations given PanAm's monopoly status

recommendation: At the current 50% load factor, introducing a Kansas City stopover allows PanAm to consolidate three West Coast aircraft into two on each KC-to-East-Coast leg, raising load factor from 50% to 75% and meaningfully improving aircraft utilization and revenue per aircraft.
PanAm should proceed with the KC stopover as long as load factors remain below 66.7%, since above that threshold consolidation no longer reduces aircraft requirements.
risks: If demand grows and load factors exceed 66.7%, the consolidation benefit disappears and the stopover only adds cost and passenger inconvenience.
Longer travel times could erode customer satisfaction and open the door for future competition on direct routes.
Operating costs at the KC hub (landing fees, turnaround time, crew) must be modeled explicitly before committing.
next_steps: Model demand forecast for West Coast routes over the next 3–5 years to assess how quickly load factors may approach the 66.7% threshold.
Conduct a full cost-benefit analysis incorporating KC stopover operating costs against aircraft savings.
Assess whether Kansas City presents any longer-term hub or network expansion opportunity to further justify the infrastructure investment.
